**Summary.** This paper presents Backline, a novel framework designed to bridge the gap between high-level quantum algorithm design in Python and the low-latency execution demands of fault-tolerant quantum computing. By compiling workloads through MLIR, it enables seamless, vendor-agnostic execution across CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs. The results demonstrate microsecond-scale synchronous co-processing, which is crucial for realizing utility-scale quantum systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it tackles the critical engineering bottleneck of scaling quantum computation by providing the necessary software stack to manage heterogeneous, low-latency classical control required for fault tolerance.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is transitioning quantum workloads from research prototypes to production-grade, fault-tolerant systems requiring extremely low-latency classical control.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrated microsecond-scale synchronous co-processing by compiling and executing quantum-classical workloads across CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs using a novel framework.

**Method.** They introduced Backline, a heterogeneous compilation and runtime framework that allows high-level Python programming to compile down through MLIR to execute on diverse, low-latency hardware accelerators.

**Model / system.** The system targets Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC) architectures, requiring tight feedback loops for Quantum Error Correction (QEC). The physical demonstration uses an AMD VPK120 FPGA board controlling communication over RoCE v2 to an AMD Ryzen CPU and AMD Instinct GPU.

**Key observables.** Median steady-state round-trip latencies (e.g., 2.305 $\mu$s to CPU, 4.5 $\mu$s to GPU) and cycle-accurate RTT profiling.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Latency budgets for QEC decoders (1 ns–1 $\mu$s for real-time control) and the ability to handle various message-issuing cadences (back-to-back vs. random-delayed).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The framework assumes the ability to abstract hardware complexity while maintaining control over low-level timing requirements, and the benchmarking relies on dedicated hardware-paced measurement paths.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the high-level compilation flow, state transition diagrams for the hardware orchestrator, and comparative traces showing how steady-state latencies shift when varying the message-issuing cadence (e.g., random-delayed vs. back-to-back).

**Paper structure.** The paper details the necessity of the framework (QEC/hardware constraints), the existing tools (PennyLane/Catalyst), the technical design of Backline for interop, and concludes with detailed usage demonstrations and benchmarks.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Moving from quantum research and development to production-grade, fault-tolerant quantum workload execution remains one of the most significant challenges facing quantum platform builders. While Python frameworks have enabled an easy entry point for quantum algorithm design, the low-latency requirements for real-time quantum error correction (QEC) demand performance that traditional interpreted environments cannot provide. FPGAs and ASICs play a central role at these layers, but their specialized programming models make development rigid and time-consuming. CPUs, GPUs, and other accelerators introduce a different challenge: as infrastructure becomes increasingly heterogeneous, programming across different devices and their associated abstractions becomes more complex. Allowing researchers to write workloads in high-level languages that map to low-latency execution across diverse distributed target platforms will enable the development of key infrastructure for utility-scale quantum systems. For this, we introduce $\textit{Backline}$, a heterogeneous compilation and runtime framework built within PennyLane and Catalyst. Backline allows us to design and build quantum-classical workloads for high-performance and low-latency devices, with compilation directly from a Python interface through MLIR. We demonstrate the compilation and execution of several quantum workloads with low-latency data movement across a mix of CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs, for both local and distributed remote hardware targets, all from a vendor-agnostic Python frontend. With an AMD VPK120 FPGA board as the controller, issuing each round from its hardware-handshake engine, we measured median steady-state round-trip latencies over RoCE v2 of $2.305~μ$s to an AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO CPU and $4.5~μ$s to an AMD Instinct MI210 GPU across $10^6-1$ rounds per path, demonstrating microsecond-scale synchronous co-processing.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a semi-device-independent method to certify the quantum randomness generated by semiconductor spin noise. By using SDP constrained only by measurable energy bounds, the authors demonstrate high, record-breaking entropy rates from quantum dot and GaAs spin noise sources. This advances the field by providing a practical, model-agnostic certification for solid-state quantum random number generators.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the practical implementation of quantum information protocols by providing a robust, model-independent certification method for a solid-state quantum source, bridging theory and experimental quantum optics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is certifying the quantum randomness generated by complex solid-state spin noise sources without needing a full, microscopic model of the underlying physics.

**Main result.** The authors achieved high certified entropy rates (up to 3.4 Gbit/s for quantum dots) from spin noise, significantly exceeding previous benchmarks.

**Method.** They employ a semi-device-independent (SDI) certification framework using Semidefinite Programming (SDP) to bound the conditional min-entropy, constrained only by measurable quantities like mean-photon-number bounds.

**Model / system.** The system utilizes semiconductor spin noise from platforms like (In,Ga)As quantum-dot ensembles and n-GaAs epilayers, measured via homodyne detection.

**Key observables.** Certified entropy rate ($h^*_{	ext{cert}}$), mean-photon-number bound ($ar{n}$), and measured noise variances ($\sigma^2$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Achieved rates: 3.2–3.4 Gbit/s (QD) and 33 Mbit/s (GaAs); the certification tolerates resolved source energy contributions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on rigorous Fock-space truncation and assumes the source is constrained by an experimentally tested mean-photon-number bound, rather than requiring full microscopic knowledge.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the certification architecture, compare different spectral regimes (broadband vs. matched mode), and show the experimental setup using balanced photoreceivers.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem, details the SDI certification methodology using SDP, presents results across multiple solid-state platforms (QD and GaAs), and concludes with performance comparisons against other QRNG sources.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Complex solid-state systems are promising platforms for scalable, high-bandwidth quantum random-number generation, yet certifying the quantum origin of their fluctuations remains difficult because the underlying microscopic dynamics are hard to model and validate. Here we demonstrate semi-device-independent quantum randomness certification from semiconductor spin noise, to our knowledge the first such certificate on any spin-noise source, without relying on a microscopic model of the spin system. The untrusted optical source is constrained by an experimentally tested mean-photon-number bound together with a declared analogue-range and per-sample clipping ceiling, while the trusted receiver is described as a calibrated, noisy, coarse-grained homodyne measurement. Using a semidefinite programme with rigorously controlled Fock-space truncation, we certify randomness that remains private against an adversary holding arbitrary quantum side information. Offline analysis yields certified entropy rates of $3.2$--$3.4$\,Gbit/s from a singly charged (In,Ga)As quantum-dot ensemble and $33$\,Mbit/s from $n$-GaAs in a spin-noise-matched detection mode. This exceeds the certified entropy rate of earlier spin-noise generators by more than two orders of magnitude, and the certificate tolerates a resolved per-symbol energy contribution from the solid-state emitter itself rather than requiring a near-vacuum input.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper advances the theory of nonreciprocal quantum batteries by replacing an inconsistent theoretical framework with a mathematically rigorous cascaded open quantum systems formalism. The authors demonstrate a significant improvement in energy storage efficiency, achieving a sixteen-fold advantage over prior benchmarks. This establishes a reliable theoretical foundation for high-performance quantum energy storage devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses open quantum systems dynamics, energy harvesting, and the rigorous mathematical treatment of dissipation, which are core topics in AMO physics and quantum optics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a mathematically rigorous framework for nonreciprocal quantum batteries that surpasses previously reported energy accumulation benchmarks.

**Main result.** The authors achieved a regime-independent sixteen-fold steady-state nonreciprocal energy advantage over reciprocal systems, establishing the cascaded formalism as the correct physical foundation.

**Method.** The study employs the rigorously established cascaded open quantum systems formalism, using the Lindblad master equation to model energy transfer dynamics.

**Model / system.** The model consists of a quantum battery and a charger, both modeled as single-mode harmonic oscillators coupled to a shared reservoir, governed by a Lindblad master equation.

**Key observables.** Energy Storage Capacity ($E_b(t)$), Useful Work (Ergotropy, $W_b(t)$), and Battery-to-Charger Energy Efficiency ($\eta$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Damping rates ($\kappa_a, \kappa_b$), coupling strengths, and the ratio of these rates ($\kappa_a/\kappa_b$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that the cascaded formalism provides the correct physical description, correcting inconsistencies found in the Metelmann–Clerk formalism.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the QB model, showing energy efficiency vs. time under various damping conditions, comparing nonreciprocal versus reciprocal energy storage.

**Paper structure.** The paper critiques prior work using the Metelmann–Clerk formalism, introduces the cascaded open quantum systems approach, derives time-dependent solutions for energy and efficiency, and compares the results against the established benchmarks.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Nonreciprocal quantum batteries harness reservoir engineering for controlled energy transfer, heralding a paradigm shift for quantum energy storage. A prior study utilizing the Metelmann-Clerk formalism reported a fourfold enhancement in nonreciprocal energy accumulation over reciprocal counterparts. This fourfold enhancement, however, appears to stem from a Lindblad master equation that exhibits fundamental inconsistencies, which may systematically understate the actual nonreciprocal advantage. Our approach is rooted in the rigorously established cascaded open quantum systems formalism, which ensures both mathematical consistency and physical fidelity. Remarkably, we surpass the previously reported fourfold benchmark, attaining a regime-independent sixteenfold steady-state nonreciprocal energy advantage over reciprocal systems. We further uncover a dissipation-dependent battery-to-charger efficiency, fourfold under symmetric damping, surpassing this benchmark when the battery is less dissipative, and lower otherwise. This work establishes the cascaded formalism as a mathematically rigorous and experimentally viable foundation for high-performance quantum energy storage.

</details>

**Summary.** This work rigorously determines the parameter regimes, particularly the inverse temperature $eta$, for which the Gibbs state of interacting fermions remains convex-Gaussian. It achieves this by developing distinct perturbative methods for both weak and strong coupling limits of the Fermi-Hubbard model. The findings provide deep structural insights into the quantum phases of correlated electron systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous characterization of when quantum states retain simple mathematical structures (like being convex combinations of Gaussian states) is crucial for understanding entanglement structure and computational complexity in strongly correlated quantum materials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the conditions under which the Gibbs state of weakly perturbed interacting fermionic systems remains convex-Gaussian.

**Main result.** It establishes precise, distinct bounds on the inverse temperature ($eta$) for convex-Gaussianity in both the weak-coupling (perturbing around free fermions) and strong-coupling (perturbing around atomic limits) regimes of the Fermi-Hubbard model.

**Method.** The analysis employs perturbation theory, utilizing Majorana operators and establishing membership in the Convex-Gaussian Cone (FGC) through structured expansions and inductive proofs.

**Model / system.** The primary model is the Fermi-Hubbard model, $H = tH_{	ext{hop}} + U V_{	ext{int}}$, studied on a general graph. The analysis is generalized to sparse Hamiltonians $H=H_0+V$ where $H_0$ is quadratic.

**Key observables.** Convex-Gaussianity of the Gibbs state $ho_eta$, and the expectation values of dressed single-string factors.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Inverse temperature ($eta$), hopping strength ($|t|$), interaction strength ($|U|$), and the coupling ratio $\epsilon = |U|/(4|t|)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is restricted to specific perturbative regimes (weak or strong coupling) and relies on the Hamiltonian being sparse or having specific structural properties.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the distinct weak-coupling and strong-coupling boundaries for the 2D Fermi-Hubbard model, showing the parameter regimes where convex-Gaussianity is maintained.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops results sequentially: first for general sparse Hamiltonians, then applying these results to derive specific bounds for the weak-coupling regime, and finally developing a separate framework for the strong-coupling regime.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the structure of Gibbs states in weakly perturbed interacting fermionic systems. First, for a sparse Hamiltonian $H=H_0+V$ with a quadratic term $H_0$ and a non-quadratic perturbation $V$ of scale $ε$, we show that the Gibbs state $ρ_β$ decomposes into a convex combination of Gaussian states whenever the inverse temperature satisfies $β\le O(\log(1/ε))$. Moreover, we prove that this bound is asymptotically tight by establishing that $β\le Θ(\log(1/ε))$ is necessary for certain sparse Hamiltonians. This general framework applies directly to the weak-coupling (small-$\vert{}U\vert{}$) regime of the Fermi--Hubbard model with hopping $t$ and on-site interaction $U$ on any graph of maximum degree $D$. Complementarily, in the strong-coupling (small-$\vert{}t\vert{}$) regime, we show that the Gibbs state remains convex-Gaussian up to $β\le O\big(\vert{}U\vert{}^{-1}\log(\vert{}U\vert{}/(D\vert{}t\vert{}))\big)$, revealing a mechanism for convex-Gaussianity distinct from the weak-coupling setting.

</details>

**Summary.** This work tackles the quantum limits for imaging with large interferometer arrays by treating the problem as a collective multiparameter estimation task. It shows that optimal measurement requires a global, collective receiver, which significantly beats standard pairwise measurements. The results provide actionable design guidelines, including a threshold determining when distributed entanglement surpasses direct optical links.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides concrete quantum limits and design targets for quantum sensing in large-scale optical arrays, directly relevant to quantum optics and quantum metrology.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper formulates and solves the multiparameter quantum estimation problem for aperture synthesis using an M-station optical array.

**Main result.** A collective receiver measurement significantly outperforms pairwise receivers, and the optimal entanglement allocation follows a square-root law favoring low-visibility baselines.

**Method.** The analysis uses the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) matrix, comparing the Holevo bound to the achievable variance using collective measurement strategies.

**Model / system.** The system is an M-station optical interferometry setup analyzing the coherence matrix G to estimate the brightness distribution I(s) across multiple baselines.

**Key observables.** Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) matrix, mean Uhlmann curvature, weighted parameter variance, and the incompatibility factor R.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The break-even baseline (L*), the entanglement resource factor f(r) = r/(1+r), and the number of stations M.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the weak thermal light assumption and neglects several effects like transmission loss and finite detector efficiency.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the incompatibility R for point vs. extended sources, compare weighted parameter variance for different receivers (collective vs. pairwise), and show the crossover defining the entanglement advantage threshold L*.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from formulating the multiparameter QFI problem, deriving the reduction lemma, comparing measurement strategies (collective vs. pairwise), determining the resource threshold, and finally solving the optimal entanglement allocation as a convex program.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Entanglement-assisted optical interferometry promises diffraction-limited imaging over baselines where light cannot be physically combined, but existing theory treats only a single visibility on one two-station baseline. This work formulates the multiparameter estimation problem for an M-station array imaging an extended scene. A reduction lemma shows that the multimode quantum Fisher information (QFI) equals the mean photon number times the QFI of a single delocalized photon, collapsing the problem to a finite-dimensional one. The local photon-number superselection rule (SSR) erases all phase information from the bare state, while shared entanglement restores a fraction f(r)=r/(1+r) of the QFI on a baseline supplied with r pairs -- a factor shown to be achievable, since the reduced two-mode state of any pair is exactly the two-station weak-thermal state. The QFI matrix and its mean Uhlmann curvature reveal numerically that a point source is measurement-compatible, whereas for every extended-source model examined it is incompatible, the Holevo bound exceeding the symmetric-logarithmic-derivative (SLD) bound by up to ~74%. An explicit collective receiver -- a global mode-sorting (quantum Fourier transform) measurement -- then attains a weighted variance within ~7% of the SLD bound and roughly an order of magnitude below an explicit pairwise receiver, and a noisy-resource advantage threshold gives the break-even baseline (~20 km for near-term parameters) beyond which repeater-distributed entanglement beats direct transmission. Finally, the optimal allocation of a finite entanglement budget is a convex program with a closed-form proportional (square-root-law) solution favoring low-visibility baselines. These results recast quantum aperture synthesis as collective multiparameter estimation and give concrete design targets, illustrated on the CHARA array.

</details>

**Summary.** This work provides a comprehensive numerical and analytical study of the Abelian sandpile model on multiple lattices, aiming to characterize its universal correlations. By employing advanced sampling techniques and comparing results against Logarithmic CFT predictions, the authors confirm consistent scaling behavior across different geometries, including a first systematic study on the kagome lattice.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the study of critical phenomena, scaling laws, and the connection to CFT provides deep insights into non-equilibrium dynamics and critical exponents, which are foundational concepts in quantum many-body physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the universal correlations and statistical properties of the Abelian sandpile model (ASM) on various 2D lattices.

**Main result.** The numerical and analytical results confirm that the ASM exhibits universal scaling behavior consistent with predictions from Logarithmic Conformal Field Theory (LCFT) across square, honeycomb, and kagome lattices.

**Method.** The authors combine advanced numerical sampling techniques (Wilson's algorithm with Majumdar-Dhar bijection) with analytical derivations using lattice Green functions to study bulk correlation functions.

**Model / system.** The system is the Abelian sandpile model (ASM) defined on planar lattices (square, honeycomb, kagome). The dynamics are governed by local toppling rules, and the focus is on the resulting recurrent, stable configurations.

**Key observables.** Bulk correlation functions (two-point), height probabilities (e.g., height-1 probability), and universal scaling exponents ($\Delta$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The lattice structure (coordination number $z$) and the correlation length $\xi 	o \infty$ (criticality).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the validity of the LCFT framework for describing the critical scaling limit, and for the kagome lattice, specific regularization choices for Green function calculations are made.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the sandpile dynamics, the Majumdar–Dhar burning bijection, and show data plots of rescaled correlation functions versus $\log r$ or $\log^2 r$ for the kagome lattice.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the ASM and its recurrence properties, establishing the mapping between recurrent configurations and spanning trees, presenting numerical studies on multiple lattices, and finally deriving analytical results for specific lattice types like the kagome lattice via Green functions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We numerically study the bulk correlation functions in the two-dimensional Abelian sandpile model, aiming both to compare with the predictions of logarithmic conformal field theory and to extend the analysis to lattices where analytical methods are difficult to apply. Wilson's algorithm efficiently generates large-scale uniform spanning trees in parallel, which can be mapped to independent recurrent configurations via the Majumdar--Dhar burning bijection, eliminating sample autocorrelations and yielding fast convergence. On the square (single-sublattice) and honeycomb (two-sublattice) lattices our results agree well with the analytical predictions. For the kagome lattice we provide the first systematic numerical study of the bulk correlation functions, and cross-check the bulk height-1 probability against a closed-form analytical expression that we also derive here via the lattice Green function.

</details>

**Summary.** This work proposes utilizing dual-unitary circuits as a superior physical platform for Quantum Reservoir Computing. By leveraging the inherent properties of dual-unitarity, the authors demonstrate enhanced memory retention and nonlinear processing power while simultaneously improving robustness against quantum noise. This bridges advanced quantum circuit design with practical quantum machine learning applications.

**Why it may be interesting.** The connection between the mathematical structure of dual-unitary operators (a topic in quantum control/geometry) and the practical requirements of machine learning (QRC) provides a deep theoretical link between quantum information theory and artificial intelligence.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper explores using dual-unitary (DU) circuits as a novel, physically realizable platform for Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC). It aims to show that this specific circuit structure enhances the performance of QRC compared to generic quantum circuits.

**Main result.** DU circuits are shown to improve memory effects, enhance nonlinear processing capabilities, and provide inherent protection against finite-shot noise compared to standard reservoir models.

**Method.** The analysis combines theoretical characterization of DU properties with numerical verification of QRC performance metrics, such as Information Processing Capacity (IPC).

**Model / system.** The model is a quantum reservoir built using a 1D lattice of qubits evolving under a Floquet unitary $U_F$, which is constructed from a core gate $V$ based on the XXZ spin chain Hamiltonian. The QRC process follows an erase-input protocol.

**Key observables.** Memory effects (related to solitons), nonlinear processing capability, protection against exponential concentration, and Information Processing Capacity (IPC).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Anisotropy ($J_z$), Trotter step ($\Delta t$), and on-site disorder ($\epsilon$). Specific regimes include interacting integrable ($\epsilon=0, \Delta t=\pi/4$) and chaotic regimes.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the assumption that the DU property provides a beneficial structure for the reservoir dynamics, and it uses the folded representation for analyzing the unitary evolution.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the general QRC protocol flow. Figure 2 shows a dynamical phase diagram mapping out different operational regimes based on system parameters. Figure 3 details the full QRC protocol flow (Washout $ightarrow$ Training $ightarrow$ Validation).

**Paper structure.** The paper reviews the QRC protocol, investigates the role of dual-unitarity and the Trotter step, analyzes memory effects via solitons, examines nonlinear processing, and concludes by quantifying the noise resilience of the DU platform.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) is a machine learning approach which employs the internal dynamics of a physical system (the reservoir) to encode and process information. In this work, we explore the use of dual-unitary circuits in a brickwork architecture as a platform for QRC, well suited to current noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. Dual-unitary circuits present both practical and conceptual advantages. Our results indicate that, under appropriate conditions, dual-unitarity can lead to an enhanced regime of operation: we numerically verify that it improves memory effects and nonlinear processing, and shields against finite-shot noise, mitigating exponential concentration. Moreover, dual unitarity offers an intuitive picture of how operator dynamics gives rise to memory and nonlinear processing in circuit-based reservoirs.

</details>

**Summary.** This work models the phase separation of soft repulsive spherocylinders confined to a sphere under non-equilibrium conditions (2-TIPS). Using MD simulations, the authors demonstrate that confinement alters the phase diagram, leading to dense-dilute coexistence. The research highlights the critical role of curvature in suppressing expected nematic ordering, providing valuable insights for soft matter physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** The study provides insights into how geometric confinement (spherical curvature) fundamentally modifies phase separation dynamics, offering analogies to non-equilibrium processes relevant in active matter and complex fluids.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the 2-Temperature induced phase separation (2-TIPS) in a system of soft repulsive spherocylinders confined on a spherical surface.

**Main result.** The system exhibits phase separation into coexisting dense and dilute regions, with confinement significantly altering the expected phase behavior, such as suppressing nematic ordering.

**Method.** Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations were employed in the NVT ensemble, utilizing a 2-temperature framework to model non-equilibrium activity.

**Model / system.** The system consists of soft repulsive spherocylinders (SRS) confined either as a spherical monolayer or a spherical shell. Interactions are modeled using the WCA potential, and the non-equilibrium state is induced by coupling subsystems at different temperatures.

**Key observables.** Phase separation extent quantified by the order parameter $\varphi$, local density distribution, and orientational ordering analyzed via the probability density distribution of the angle $\psi$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Packing fraction ($\eta$), rod aspect ratio ($A$), and the activity difference ($\chi$) are key parameters varied across different confinement geometries.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the validity of the 2-temperature model for inducing non-equilibrium activity and notes limitations regarding the systematic study of the nematic phase across all aspect ratios.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the coexisting dense/dilute regions (hot/cold) upon 2-TIPS, showing defect structures and the bimodal density distribution confirming phase coexistence.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically compares results between free and tangential anchoring conditions on the spherical surface, detailing the phase separation mechanism and contrasting the findings with bulk 3D systems.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We studied the 2-Temperature induced phase separation (2-TIPS) in a system of soft repulsive sphe rocylinders (SRS), confined on the surface of a sphere. We used two different anchoring conditions for the SRS on the spherical surface- free and tangential. For the free anchoring, increasing either the packing fraction or the rod aspect ratio suppresses phase separation between the active and passive subsystems, and the system corresponds to a dense-dilute phase co-existence. These phenomena can be explained via the trapping effect and are emergent due to the confinement. For the tangential anchoring, the system phase separates from its initial isotropic state into a locally ordered dense region and a disordered dilute region. Our work provides useful insights into phase separation in binary mixtures under spherical confinement.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a method to find optimal time-dependent Hamiltonians that significantly improve the convergence of free energy estimates derived from non-equilibrium simulations. By minimizing the Mean Squared Error (MSE) of the Jarzynski estimator for Markov models, the authors show that these optimal Hamiltonians can drastically outperform simple linear or logarithmic interpolations. This offers a powerful new tool for calculating free energy barriers in complex physical systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides concrete, computationally derived heuristics for improving non-equilibrium free energy calculations, which is crucial for simulating processes in molecular dynamics and condensed matter systems where rare events dominate.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the poor convergence of free energy estimates derived from non-equilibrium, finite-time switching simulations using the Jarzynski relation.

**Main result.** Optimal intermediate Hamiltonians, determined by minimizing the Mean Squared Error (MSE), can reduce the MSE by over an order of magnitude compared to simple interpolations.

**Method.** The authors use gradient-based minimization techniques applied to an exact tilted-master-equation representation of the MSE for discrete-time Markov models.

**Model / system.** The study uses discrete-time Markov models defined on a line of $m$ states, whose evolution is governed by a time-dependent Hamiltonian $H(x, 	au)$ within a master equation framework.

**Key observables.** Mean Squared Error (MSE) of the Jarzynski estimator, mean work ($\langle W angle$), and mean position ($\langle x angle$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The complexity is varied by changing the number of states ($m$), the depth ($\delta$) of the potential well, and the number of intermediate steps ($N$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is restricted to discrete-time Markov models, and the optimization relies on the large-sample limit ($n \gg 1$) for the MSE calculation.

**Figures summary.** Figures systematically compare the calculated mean position ($\langle x angle$) and the MSE for various intermediate Hamiltonians (optimal vs. linear/logarithmic) across different model parameters ($\delta, m, N$).

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the problem using the Jarzynski relation for Markov models. It then develops the mathematical framework to minimize the MSE using tilted-master-equations. Finally, it applies this method to complex model systems like the shifted potential well, comparing optimal results against standard interpolation schemes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Jarzynski relation enables the estimation of equilibrium free energy differences from non-equilibrium, finite-time switching simulations. These estimates usually converge poorly because rare trajectories dominate the exponential work average. Here, we numerically determined and explored the sequence of intermediate Hamiltonians connecting initial and final states that minimize the mean squared error (MSE) of the Jarzynski estimator and thereby enhance convergence. For discrete-time Markov models, an exact tilted-master-equation representation of the MSE in the large-sample limit, combined with automatic differentiation, enables efficient gradient-based minimization over all intermediate energies. We applied our approach to three model systems of increasing complexity: a two-state model, a double-well potential, and a shifted potential well. In all three systems, the optimal intermediate Hamiltonians jump at the initial and final times. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations show that optimal intermediates can reduce the MSE by more than an order of magnitude compared with linear and logarithmic interpolation, most strongly for large changes in the energy landscape. Remarkably, they need not dissipate less work than intermediates yielding larger errors. Our results suggest heuristics for more efficient non-equilibrium free energy calculations of realistic molecular systems: optimal intermediate Hamiltonians jump at the initial and final times; for barrier-crossing problems, the barrier should be lowered rapidly and raised again later; and minimizing dissipation does not guarantee faster convergence.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously demonstrates that the self-testing of maximally entangled qubit strategies is not robust when restricted only to full-rank Projective Measurements (PVMs). By constructing a specific nonlocal game, the authors show that optimal correlations achievable with nonprojective measurements are fundamentally different from those achievable under the strict PVM assumption.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a deep theoretical understanding of the limitations of self-testing protocols in quantum information theory, showing that imposing physical constraints (like projectivity) can fundamentally alter the set of achievable correlations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the robustness of self-testing protocols for maximally entangled qubit strategies when restricted to pure, full-Schmidt-rank Projective Measurements (PVMs). It aims to resolve a conjecture regarding the simultaneous imposition of full rank and projectivity.

**Main result.** The authors prove a separation: an optimal strategy using a nonprojective measurement can be found that does not admit a local dilation to the reference state, demonstrating that the full-rank PVM self-test is not robust.

**Method.** The analysis constructs a nonlocal game $H$ combining CHSH with an auxiliary game $G$. The core method involves comparing the algebraic structure of optimal correlations derived from PVMs versus those from nonprojective measurements, utilizing local dilation concepts.

**Model / system.** The study uses qubits ($\mathbb{C}^2 \otimes \mathbb{C}^2$) and the maximally entangled state $|\Phi^+angle$ within the framework of nonlocal games. The analysis heavily relies on the algebraic structure of optimal correlations, involving $C^*$-algebras like $C \oplus M_2(C)$.

**Key observables.** The quantum value ($\omega_q(H)$) and classical value ($\omega_c(H)$) of the constructed game $H$; the local dilation error.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The parameter $t \in (0, 1)$ controlling the deviation from the reference state; the specific correlation values like $19/22$ and $71/88$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The argument hinges on the algebraic difference between deterministic optima (from projectivity) and trine optima (from nonprojectivity) in the auxiliary game $G$.

**Paper structure.** The paper first analyzes the auxiliary game $G$ to establish a discrepancy between its projective and nonprojective optima. It then combines $G$ with the CHSH game to construct $H$, culminating in the proof of the separation theorem showing the non-robustness of the PVM self-test.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We construct a nonlocal game that self-tests a maximally entangled qubit strategy among pure full-Schmidt-rank projective strategies, but admits an inequivalent optimum using one nonprojective measurement. This resolves a conjecture of Baptista et al. on imposing full rank and projectivity simultaneously. The construction combines CHSH with an auxiliary game $G$ that forces deterministic answers under these assumptions and admits a trine POVM optimum without them. We classify the optimal correlations of $G$ as a line segment parametrized by the tracial states of $\mathbb{C}\oplus M_2(\mathbb{C})$. Projectivity on the state support removes the matrix summand, whereas projective dilations with nonzero nonabort probability have a nontracial local state whose zero left ideal is not two-sided. Finally, a family in local dimension six shows that the full-rank PVM self-test is not robust.

</details>

**Summary.** This work proposes a novel Bell test framework for analyzing data from particle collider decays. It tackles the inherent loophole caused by postselection by requiring operational equivalence across measurement settings. A violation of the derived Bell inequality provides evidence for quantum nonlocality or measurement contextuality in this high-energy physics context.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on particle physics, the rigorous development of contextuality constraints based on operational equivalence in a measurement setting is highly relevant to foundational quantum information theory and loophole-free tests.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper develops a framework to perform Bell tests using data recorded from high-energy collider decays, addressing the challenge of measurement settings being determined by detector acceptance rather than freely chosen.

**Main result.** A violation of a derived Bell inequality, under assumptions of measurement independence and operational equivalence, witnesses either Bell nonlocality or joint-acceptance contextuality.

**Method.** The authors derive a continuous-input Bell inequality and analyze the loophole opened by postselection, showing that operational equivalence constrains local hidden variable models.

**Model / system.** The system involves the decay of unstable qubits in a collider, where daughter momenta act as spin analyzers. The test uses independently sampled analysis axes to define accepted spherical caps for binary outcomes.

**Key observables.** The Bell functional B = -<x . y a b>, the local acceptance probability q_A, and the joint acceptance event D.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Spin-analyzing power (eta_A), the cap radius (phi), and the bound violation condition mu_A mu_B > 3/4.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Measurement independence (lambda-independence) and the operational equivalence of joint-acceptance events across all settings are crucial assumptions.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the geometric coarse-graining defined by the analysis axis, showing the accepted caps (+1, -1) and the no-click region (empty set).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the Bell test framework for collider data, addressing the postselection loophole, deriving the contextuality constraint via operational equivalence, and finally presenting the specific Bell inequality and its quantum prediction.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose Bell tests for collider decays using independently sampled analysis axes as settings and detector regions to assign binary or null outcomes. We show that a Bell violation requires postselection, opening a loophole. However, under measurement independence and operational equivalence of acceptance events across settings, any local model exploiting the loophole must be nonclassical in the sense of measurement contextuality. We derive a Bell inequality violated by singlet correlations when the effective spin-analyzing powers are sufficiently high. Its violation then witnesses Bell nonlocality or measurement contextuality.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a theoretical framework showing that error suppression during magic-state cultivation can be modeled exactly by a binary linear code. By using coded Clifford measurements, the authors demonstrate substantial physical savings in required resources (like gate steps and active locations) compared to naive repetition schemes. This provides a concrete, resource-efficient pathway for building fault-tolerant quantum computation.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on quantum computation, the rigorous application of coding theory bounds (like the Plotkin bound) to physical measurement constraints provides a powerful theoretical framework for optimizing resource overhead in any complex quantum system.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the need for efficient, fault-tolerant methods to cultivate necessary quantum resources, specifically magic states, by suppressing errors through measurement of logical Clifford symmetries.

**Main result.** Implementing the measurement schedule using coded Clifford observables allows for significant resource savings (e.g., 26.6% reduction in active locations) compared to independent repetition schedules, while maintaining the required error suppression distance.

**Method.** The authors map the error-suppressing measurement process onto a binary linear code structure, using commuting Hermitian Clifford observables derived from the resource state symmetries.

**Model / system.** The model is fault-tolerant quantum computation, focusing on resource state preparation (magic states like $|CSangle$ and $|CCZangle$) and error correction via measurement of logical symmetries within the Clifford group $\mathcal{C}_3$.

**Key observables.** Record-error fault order ($d_{	ext{record}}$), active locations, qubit-steps, and the resulting logical error probability $P_{	ext{wv}} = O(q^d)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Code distance ($d$), resource type ($|CSangle, |CCZangle$), and the physical error rate ($p$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis focuses on the logical-level code-cultivation correspondence, and the results are noted to be diagnostics rather than full-factory logical-error estimates.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the logical-level code-cultivation correspondence, quantifying resource reductions (e.g., gate steps, logical checks) achieved by coded schedules versus independent repetition schedules for various resource types.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the link between error suppression and linear codes, derives the measurement observables $C(v)$, compares resource costs (active locations/qubit-steps) between coded and non-coded methods, and concludes with optimization results for minimum-cost schedules.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Magic-state cultivation suppresses errors by measuring logical Clifford symmetries and discarding inconsistent outcomes. For an entangled resource several branches are accepted, so the retained branch carries a multibit classical record whose corruption produces a logical-frame error. We show that this record layer is exactly a binary linear code. For any third-level Clifford-hierarchy unitary $U \in \mathcal{C}_3$, the branches $UZ(a)|+\rangle^{\otimes k}$ are resolved by commuting Hermitian Clifford observables $C(v) = UX(v)U^{\dagger}$, so a measurement schedule is a generator matrix and postselection on valid records gives $P_{\mathrm{wv}} = O(q^{d})$ at record distance $d$. A Plotkin bound then limits every binary record, linear or not. The physically realizable Clifford family already saturates it: at distance four, six logical measurements suffice for $|CS\rangle$ and seven for $|CCZ\rangle$, against eight and twelve for independent repetition. Restricting to fault-tolerantly measurable parities therefore costs nothing in record length. The saving survives compilation: in a native-CZZ-assisted Steane realization the $[6,2,4]$ CS schedule is the unique minimum-cost distance-four solution, reducing the cultivation core by 26.6\% in active locations, and exact state-vector simulation without a final ideal code-space projection confirms higher acceptance and roughly half the residual Steane-boundary weight. Coding thus reduces logical redundancy and compiled overhead together.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a novel, low-overhead scheduling framework for quantum circuits running on multi-QPU systems. It uses a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to predict the execution fidelity on various hardware devices before compilation. By incorporating a tunable weight, the scheduler effectively balances the trade-off between achieving the highest possible fidelity and maximizing the utilization of all available quantum processing units.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the practical challenges of running quantum algorithms on real, noisy, and heterogeneous hardware, which is a major bottleneck for applying quantum computing to physics simulations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is developing a scheduling framework for quantum circuits on heterogeneous multi-QPU systems that maximizes execution fidelity while balancing this fidelity against the need for high parallelism.

**Main result.** The proposed GNN-based framework successfully approximates exhaustive fidelity-based assignment, achieving significant speedups in scheduling overhead compared to brute-force methods while maintaining high mean batch fidelity.

**Method.** The authors propose an end-to-end pipeline using a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to predict the expected fidelity of a circuit on any given QPU *before* compilation. A tunable scheduler then uses this prediction to balance fidelity maximization against workload distribution.

**Model / system.** The system involves multi-QPU platforms exposed in HPCQC environments, where each QPU has unique characteristics (size, topology, noise). The input circuit is converted into a graph representation (DAG) for the GNN to process.

**Key observables.** Execution Fidelity ($f_{c,d}$), Mean Batch Fidelity, Fidelity Regret ($r(c)$), and Wall-Clock Scheduling Overhead.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The tunable scheduling weight $w \in [0, 1]$, which controls the trade-off between fidelity and parallelism.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The fidelity calculation used is an approximation that neglects factors like idle-time decoherence, crosstalk, and calibration drift.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the end-to-end pipeline, the graph conversion process, and comparisons showing mean ground-truth fidelity vs. weight $w$, and median scheduling cost comparing exhaustive vs. GNN-predicted selection.

**Paper structure.** The paper follows a structure detailing the problem (multi-QPU scheduling), presenting the solution (GNN prediction + tunable scheduler), and validating it through rigorous comparisons against exhaustive baselines regarding both fidelity and computational overhead.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

High Performance Computing-Quantum Computing (HPCQC) platforms expose multiple Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) that may differ in size, topology, native gates, and noise characteristics. For current noisy devices, errors compound along the compiled circuits quickly, and minimizing them, that is, maximizing the circuits' execution fidelity, is essential for reliable results. Fidelity depends on the compilation to a specific target device: the same high-level circuit may produce different executables and, therefore, different expected fidelities across QPUs. We present a low-overhead fidelity-aware scheduling framework for multi-QPU systems based on a Graph Neural Network (GNN) that estimates, before compilation, the expected fidelity of each circuit on each available QPU. Then, a tunable scheduler uses these estimates to control the trade-off between execution fidelity and parallelism. Results show that this framework allows for approximating an exhaustive fidelity-based assignment, saving computational resources compared to a brute-force approach that compiles each circuit on every device.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper investigates the long-time statistical behavior of a non-confined Feller process, a model exhibiting broken ergodicity. The authors derive an asymptotic factorization for the local-time field, showing its spatial structure is governed by a deterministic profile while temporal fluctuations follow a Mittag-Leffler distribution. This work establishes a unifying framework for analyzing complex, non-equilibrium dynamics in systems with singular invariant measures.

**Why it may be interesting.** The concept of infinite ergodic theory and the resulting universal scaling laws for local-time fields provide powerful mathematical tools for understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in complex physical systems, which has parallels in open quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study focuses on the spatial structure and multi-point correlation properties of the local-time field for non-confined Feller processes within the framework of Infinite Ergodic Theory.

**Main result.** The local-time field exhibits an asymptotic spatiotemporal factorization, and normalized spatial correlations converge to a universal constant independent of the observation levels.

**Method.** The analysis uses asymptotic methods, including the derivation of factorization laws and the comparison of time averages in ergodic versus non-ergodic regimes.

**Model / system.** The primary model is the non-confined Feller process, which is a diffusion process characterized by multiplicative noise and possesses a non-normalizable stationary probability density.

**Key observables.** Local-time field L(x, t), occupation times, two-point spatial cross-correlation function, and non-integrable power observables A_q(t).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The analysis is focused on the non-confined regime ($0 < 	heta < 1$) and the long-time limit ($t 	o \infty$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the process can be mapped to a squared Bessel process after deterministic rescaling, and it relies on the framework of infinite ergodic theory.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the collapse of probability density functions for occupation times and the convergence of correlation functions to universal constants.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theory by first establishing the asymptotic factorization of the local-time field, then analyzing the convergence of occupation times, and finally contrasting the scaling behavior of integrable versus non-integrable observables.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study additive observables of a non-confined Feller process characterized by a non- normalizable stationary probability density and return times with infinite mean. The process is equivalent, after a deterministic rescaling, to a squared Bessel process, but we focus here on a question: the spatial structure of its local-time field. We show that the local time admits a fac- torization in the long time limit. Its spatial profile is governed by the non-normalizable stationary density, whereas its temporal fluctuations are controlled by a single Mittag-Leffler random ampli- tude. As a consequence, normalized spatial correlations of the local time converge to a universal constant independent of the two observation levels. Occupation times of finite intervals follow as corollaries and display Darling-Kac fluctuations. In contrast, non-integrable power observables exhibit self-similar squared-Bessel-type limits rather than Mittag-Leffler statistics. This spatial- field perspective provides a unifying framework for infinite ergodic theory under state-dependent multiplicative noise.

</details>

**Summary.** This work establishes the optimal sample complexity for reconstructing low-rank quantum states using limited joint measurements. It derives a precise scaling law dependent on the state rank, ambient dimension, and the maximum number of samples per measurement. The results provide crucial theoretical benchmarks for quantum state tomography protocols.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper determines the optimal sample complexity required for low-rank quantum state tomography when measurements are restricted to jointly sampling at most $t$ instances.

**Main result.** The required sample complexity is $\Theta\left(rac{dr}{\epsilon^2} \max\left(1, rac{r}{\sqrt{t}}ight)ight)$, establishing a matching lower and upper bound.

**Method.** The lower bound uses the van Trees inequality applied to the Fisher information trace, while the upper bound constructs a nonadaptive protocol based on Gaussian joint measurements.

**Model / system.** The system is an unknown quantum state $ho$ on $\mathbb{C}^d$ assumed to have a rank of at most $r$. The goal is to estimate this state to a trace norm error $\epsilon$ using measurements that jointly sample up to $t$ instances.

**Key observables.** Trace norm error ($\epsilon$), sample complexity ($n$), Fisher information trace.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Ambient dimension ($d$), state rank ($r$), maximum joint samples ($t$), target error ($\epsilon$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the protocol can choose measurements adaptively (for the lower bound) and considers the case of sufficiently small $\epsilon$.

**Figures summary.** Not specified.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the lower bound using adaptive Fisher chain rules and the van Trees inequality, and establishes the matching upper bound via a nonadaptive Gaussian joint measurement protocol.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We determine the optimal sample complexity of low-rank quantum state tomography when each measurement may act jointly on at most $t$ samples. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, estimating an unknown state on $\mathbb{C}^d$ of rank at most $r$ to trace norm error $\varepsilon$ with constant success probability requires, and is achievable with, $$   Θ\left(   \frac{dr}{\varepsilon^2}   \max\left\{1,\frac r{\sqrt t}\right\}   \right)$$ samples. The lower bound allows the protocol to choose each joint measurement adaptively using all previous classical outcomes; the matching upper bound is nonadaptive. Thus joint measurements on at most $t$ samples improve the complexity of algorithms making single-sample measurements by at most a factor $\sqrt t$. Further, measuring order $r^2$ samples jointly is necessary and sufficient to attain the unrestricted collective rate.   For the lower bound, we vary the support of a state with fixed uniform spectrum and bound the Fisher information trace of every joint measurement on $t$ samples. The adaptive Fisher chain rule and the van Trees inequality then give the trace norm lower bound. For the upper bound, we construct and analyze a nonadaptive tomography protocol based on a Gaussian joint measurement. An explicit second moment identity and a conditional Gaussian law outside the state's support give a rank-dependent error analysis, yielding the matching rate.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper constructs a static, real-valued spin-network Hamiltonian that perfectly transfers a localized two-excitation state to the symmetric Dicke state for any system size $N \ge 4$. The existence proof is purely symbolic, relying on solving polynomial equations derived from symmetry constraints. It offers a novel, fixed-Hamiltonian approach to quantum state transfer, contrasting with time-dependent or measurement-based protocols.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a purely algebraic, non-optimization-based construction for achieving quantum state transfer using a fixed Hamiltonian, which is highly valuable for designing physical quantum simulators or quantum computing architectures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to construct a time-independent, excitation-preserving spin Hamiltonian that achieves Perfect State Transfer (PST) from a localized two-excitation state to the symmetric two-excitation Dicke state for any system size $N \ge 4$.

**Main result.** The authors prove the existence of such a Hamiltonian for all $N \ge 4$ using purely symbolic mathematical methods, establishing a constrained analogue of PST.

**Method.** The construction involves exploiting an $S_{N-2}$ permutation symmetry to reduce the dynamics to a 4D subspace, followed by solving an inverse spectral problem that reduces to finding a real root of a cubic polynomial.

**Model / system.** The system is an $N$-qubit spin chain governed by a spin-network Hamiltonian $H = \sum_{i<j} J_{ij} (\sigma_i^+ \sigma_j^- + \sigma_j^+ \sigma_i^-) + \sum_i \epsilon_i n_i$. The dynamics are confined to the two-excitation sector.

**Key observables.** The transfer fidelity, which must equal 1, and the required spectral structure $\{(-n, -1, 0, 1)\pi\}$ for the Hamiltonian eigenvalues.

**Important parameters / regimes.** System size $N \ge 4$, the odd integer parameter $n$, and the free coupling parameters determined by solving the polynomial equations.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The Hamiltonian must arise from an excitation-preserving spin-network form, which is a stricter constraint than general real symmetric matrices. The result is only proven for two excitations ($k=2$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the existence of a required real root $z^* < -2$ via sign analysis (Intermediate Value Theorem) and show numerical validation of the construction for $N=4$ to $102$ with small residuals.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical problem, reduces the dynamics using symmetry, formulates the problem as an inverse spectral problem, solves the resulting polynomial equations symbolically to prove existence, and concludes by comparing this static method to other PST protocols.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

I construct a family of time-independent, excitation-preserving spin Hamiltonians that realises perfect state transfer from a localised two-excitation state to the symmetric two-excitation Dicke state, for every system size $N \ge 4$. The Hamiltonian has the physical form $H = \sum_{i<j} J_{ij} (σ_i^+ σ_j^- + σ_j^+ σ_i^-) + \sum_i ε_i n_i$ with real couplings, and satisfies $e^{-iHt} |110\cdots0\rangle = e^{iφ} |D_N^{(2)}\rangle$ at a finite time. The construction exploits an $S_{N-2}$ permutation symmetry acting on the initially unoccupied spins, which reduces the dynamics to a four-dimensional invariant subspace. Requiring $(|ψ_0\rangle + |D_N^{(2)}\rangle)/2$ to be a zero eigenvector determines the on-site energies in closed form and leaves three coupling parameters free. The remaining inverse spectral problem reduces to two polynomial equations in two dimensionless coupling ratios; eliminating one ratio yields a degree-six reciprocal polynomial, which the substitution $z = x + x^{-1}$ converts to a cubic. For the spectral family $(-n,-1,1)$, with $n$ an odd integer, an explicit factorisation of the leading coefficient together with a boundary evaluation at $z=-2$ shows that for every $N \ge 4$ an odd $n$ can be chosen large enough that a real root with $z < -2$ exists; a subresultant argument supplies a real lift of that root to the original system. The existence proof is entirely symbolic and does not rely on numerical optimisation; direct propagation is used only as independent validation. The result is a constrained analogue of perfect state transfer: unlike the general real-state problem, where an unconstrained real symmetric matrix suffices, here the Hamiltonian is required to arise from an excitation-preserving spin-network form.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops an 'information ladder' to quantify how well neutrino oscillation parameters can be measured using reactor antineutrinos at the JUNO experiment. By comparing Quantum, Flavor, and Event-level Fisher Information, the authors show that while some parameters are well-constrained, others suffer significant information loss due to detector limitations. Despite this, the remaining information is sufficient for high-precision measurements.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous application of quantum information theory (QFI) to particle physics measurements provides a powerful, general framework for assessing experimental limits, which is relevant for any field involving quantum state estimation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper quantifies how information about neutrino oscillation parameters is encoded in the quantum state and how efficiently this information can be extracted through measurement.

**Main result.** While information on solar parameters approaches the optimal statistical limit, information on $\theta_{13}$ and $\Delta m_{31}^{2}$ is significantly degraded by detector effects, though sufficient for sub-percent precision on $\Delta m_{31}^{2}$ at JUNO.

**Method.** It establishes an 'information ladder' by comparing three levels of Fisher Information: Quantum Fisher Information (QFI), classical flavor Fisher information, and event-level Fisher information.

**Model / system.** The analysis uses the framework of neutrino oscillations, specifically modeling reactor antineutrino states propagating to the JUNO detector baseline.

**Key observables.** The relative information retained at different levels ($	ext{e}F_{	ext{flavor}}/	ext{e}F_{	ext{Q}}$ and $F_{	ext{event}}/F_{	ext{Q}}$) and the resulting $1\sigma$ precision for the oscillation parameters.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Oscillation parameters: $\theta_{12}, \theta_{13}, \Delta m_{21}^2, \Delta m_{31}^2$. The analysis is performed for the JUNO setup (20 kton, 52.5 km, 6 years).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis models energy resolution using a Gaussian function and neglects matter effects in some calculations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the energy dependence of the diagonal Fisher-information elements for the four parameters across the three information levels, showing the hierarchy and parameter dependence.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theoretical framework by deriving the QFI matrix elements, compares this to the flavor-FI derived from the survival probability, and finally incorporates detector effects to yield the event-level FI, establishing the information hierarchy.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Since neutrinos are quantum systems inherently, the precision with which oscillation parameters can be estimated ultimately depends on how much information about these parameters is encoded in the neutrino state and how efficiently that information can be extracted through measurement. In this work, we quantify how information encoded in reactor antineutrino states flows through the measurement process to the events observed at the detector, using quantum and classical Fisher information. We establish the information ladder for JUNO, revealing that the loss of precision across different information levels is strongly parameter dependent. We demonstrate that the JUNO configuration approaches the optimal statistical limit for the oscillation parameters of the solar sector, while information on $θ_{13}$ and $Δm_{31}^{2}$ is significantly degraded by the measurement strategy and detector effects. Despite this information loss, the remaining information is sufficient for JUNO to achieve sub-percent precision on $Δm_{31}^{2}$ within six years.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces SIM-GRAPH, a novel computational method that leverages underlying symmetries in quantum Hamiltonians to drastically reduce the effective size of the system being simulated. By projecting interactions onto a symmetric subspace, it achieves an exponential speedup over standard exact diagonalization for calculating ground-state properties. It is highly valuable for studying large, interacting quantum spin systems like the TFIM on various complex lattices.

**Why it may be interesting.** The technique of exploiting underlying symmetries to reduce the effective dimensionality of the Hilbert space is highly relevant for simulating complex quantum materials where symmetries are known or suspected.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is efficiently calculating ground-state observables of interacting quantum many-body systems, which typically suffer from exponentially scaling Hilbert space dimensions.

**Main result.** The SIM-GRAPH method provides an exponential speedup over standard exact diagonalization by projecting interactions onto a symmetry-reduced graph, achieving high accuracy on various lattices.

**Method.** The method, SIM-GRAPH, maps the Hamiltonian onto a graph, uses group theory to identify symmetries, and constructs a symmetry-reduced Hamiltonian by projecting interactions onto the symmetric subset of sites.

**Model / system.** The method is applied to interacting quantum many-body systems, specifically modeling the Transverse Field Ising Model (TFIM) on various lattices (1D chains, 2D square lattices, Sierpinski triangles).

**Key observables.** Ground-state observables, notably the average ground-state magnetization ($\langle n_\uparrow angle$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The ratio of transverse field ($\Omega$) to coupling strength ($\Delta$), and the size/geometry of the lattice (e.g., 3x3, 4x4).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method is projective, meaning computed eigenenergies are guaranteed to be greater than or equal to the true eigenenergies, and it assumes that the ground state can be accurately represented by the symmetric subspace.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the graph reduction process for lattices (e.g., 3x3), compare ground-state magnetization vs. field ratio for different lattices (1D and 2D), and show convergence studies using various SIM2.n methods.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces SIM-GRAPH, details its application to the TFIM on various geometries (1D, 2D, Sierpinski), and systematically compares its results against Exact Diagonalization (ED) using increasingly refined projection techniques (SIM2.n and SIM3).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Symmetry plays a central role throughout physics, from Fourier analysis on discrete lattices to the classification of elementary particles in the standard model. In finite quantum systems, symmetries are often discrete, such as reflection and rotational symmetries. Here, we present the SIM-GRAPH method (Symmetric Ising Models - Graph Reduction And Projected Hamiltonians), which uses such symmetries to efficiently calculate ground-state observables of interacting quantum systems. By projecting all interactions onto a symmetric subset of the system, the method effectively reduces the number of sites, thus providing an exponential speedup over standard exact diagonalization. Furthermore, we introduce two extensions that broaden the applicability of the method and allow for a controlled trade-off between computational cost and accuracy.

</details>

**Summary.** This work experimentally demonstrates that applying mechanical strain to the CDW material NbSe3 can tune its electronic phase transitions. By combining XRD and transport measurements, the authors establish a strong, quantifiable link between the material's lattice structure and the critical temperatures of the CDW states. This highlights the profound interplay between lattice dynamics and electronic correlations in low-dimensional conductors.

**Why it may be interesting.** The strong coupling observed between mechanical strain (a classical/structural input) and the electronic phase transition temperature (CDW) provides a tangible experimental platform for studying emergent quantum phases in correlated materials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how applying mechanical lattice strain tunes the Charge Density Wave (CDW) transitions in the quasi-one-dimensional material NbSe3.

**Main result.** The CDW critical temperatures ($T_{c1}$ and $T_{c2}$) are found to be strongly correlated with the applied lattice strain and resulting lattice parameters, demonstrating a direct coupling between structure and electronic phase transitions.

**Method.** The research combines in-situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements under uniaxial tensile stress with electrical transport measurements to probe both structural changes and electronic properties.

**Model / system.** The system is NbSe3, a prototypical quasi-one-dimensional conductor exhibiting multiple CDW transitions. The analysis involves relating macroscopic mechanical properties (Young's moduli, Poisson's coefficients) to the electronic susceptibility and CDW critical temperatures.

**Key observables.** CDW critical temperatures ($T_{c1}, T_{c2}$), lattice parameters ($a, b, c$), electrical resistance $R(T)$, and elastic constants (Young's moduli, Poisson's coefficients).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Applied tensile stresses ($\sigma_b, \sigma_c$), strain ($\epsilon$), and the characteristic temperatures of the two CDW transitions (145 K and 59 K).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes linear elastic behavior and that shear strains are negligible during the deformation process.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the evolution of lattice parameters and XRD intensities under applied stresses, and show the temperature dependence of resistance curves ($R(T)$) before and after stress application.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by first characterizing the mechanical response of NbSe3 under strain using XRD, then correlating these structural changes with the observed shifts in the CDW transition temperatures derived from transport measurements, and finally discussing the underlying electronic mechanisms.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Charge Density Wave (CDW) state is a perfect example of a combined structural and electronic state, both characterized by a periodic lattice distortion and an electronic modulation of condensed electrons, resulting from electron-phonon coupling. They are thus prone to be tuned by lattice strain. NbSe3 is a prototypical example of CDW states, with a chain-like structure displaying two CDWs at 145K and 59K, with wavevectors along and inclined with respect to the chain axis b. Here, we report on the evolution of the lattice structure and CDW properties in the quasi-one-dimensional charge-density-wave system NbSe3 under tensile stresses applied along and perpendicular to the chains axis b by a combination of X-ray diffraction and transport measurements. We find that the lattice structure show exotic Poissons coefficients and strongly anisotropic Youngs moduli while the evolution of the electrical resistance demonstrates shifts of both charge-density-wave critical temperatures that are strongly correlated with the lattice parameters. The two CDW transitions display different behaviours under applied stresses, and suggest that a modification of the band curvature leads to the observed transport signatures.

</details>

**Summary.** This work simulates the organization of multiple knots on a flexible polymer chain, comparing homogeneous and heterogeneous knot pairs. The simulations reveal that the initial topology strongly dictates whether the knots remain separated or mix into a composite state. Crucially, the heterogeneous pair shows a pronounced tendency to mix, achieving this state while occupying less polymer contour than when separated.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on polymer physics, the study uses advanced simulation techniques to characterize complex, non-equilibrium phase behavior (mixing/demixing) driven by topological constraints, which shares conceptual links with understanding entanglement in quantum many-body systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how the inherent topology of constituent knots influences the process of mixing or demixing when multiple knots are confined within a flexible polymer chain.

**Main result.** Heterogeneous knot pairs ($3_1 \otimes 5_1$) show a greater tendency to mix and achieve a composite state that occupies significantly less polymer contour than the separated state, suggesting topology dictates organizational efficiency.

**Method.** The research employs coarse-grained Brownian-dynamics simulations to track the time evolution and probability distribution of knot configurations.

**Model / system.** The system is a flexible polymer chain modeled by beads connected by harmonic springs and confined between two opposing walls using a WCA potential. Two specific knot pairs, homogeneous ($3_1 \otimes 3_1$) and heterogeneous ($3_1 \otimes 5_1$), are studied.

**Key observables.** Frequency of mixed vs. demixed configurations, contour occupancy reduction ($\Delta L$), and the boundary-based knot separation metric ($\Delta b$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Normalized wall separation ($x = d/L$), which controls the degree of end-to-end stretching.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the boundary-based metric $\Delta b$ for state classification, and simulations are performed in the overdamped limit.

**Figures summary.** Figures show the probability distribution of the knot separation coordinate ($\Delta b$) versus wall separation ($x$), and quantify the reduction in contour occupancy ($\Delta L$) upon mixing for both knot types.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically compares the dynamics of $3_1 \otimes 3_1$ and $3_1 \otimes 5_1$ pairs across varying wall separations, quantifying the transition between mixed and demixed states and measuring the structural consequences of mixing.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The organization of multiple knots along a polymer contour can depend sensitively on the topology of the constituent knots. Using coarse-grained Brownian-dynamics simulations, we investigate topology-dependent mixing of two knots in a flexible polymer at controlled normalized wall separation. We compare homogeneous ($3_1\otimes 3_1$) and heterogeneous ($3_1\otimes 5_1$) knot pairs using a contour-based coordinate that distinguishes mixed and demixed configurations. Starting from partially overlapping configurations, the $3_1\otimes 5_1$ pair is observed in mixed configurations more frequently over the simulation time window than the $3_1\otimes 3_1$ pair at intermediate wall separation. We further find that, over the intermediate range of normalized wall separation, mixing of the $3_1\otimes5_1$ pair produces a composite knotted region that occupies substantially less polymer contour than the two constituent knots collectively occupy in demixed configurations. The corresponding reduction in contour occupancy is much smaller for the $3_1\otimes3_1$ pair. This indicates that the heterogeneous constituent topologies can be accommodated within a smaller portion of the polymer contour in the composite configuration. These results establish that constituent topology can strongly influence multiple-knot organization in flexible polymers.

</details>
